title: Blockchain Network
description: Design a blockchain network — peer-to-peer gossip of transactions and blocks, a mempool, consensus and finality, state storage with Merkle proofs, and light clients.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Blockchain Network?
blocks.text: A blockchain network is a set of independently operated nodes that agree on a single ordered history of transactions without trusting any one party. Transactions are grouped into **blocks**, each linked to the previous one by a cryptographic hash, and a **consensus** protocol decides which block comes next. The interesting design problem is agreement among nodes that may be faulty or malicious.

items: Users should be able to submit signed transactions transferring value between accounts.
Nodes should agree on the order of transactions and on every account's balance.
Once a transaction is final, it should never be reversed.
Anyone should be able to run a node, and lightweight clients should be able to verify their balance without downloading everything.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Safety under Byzantine faults: correct as long as fewer than one third of validators (by stake) are malicious.
Open participation across thousands of nodes over the public internet.
**Account**: address (derived from a public key), balance, nonce.
**Transaction**: from, to, amount, nonce, fee, signature.
**Block**: header (parent hash, height, state root, transactions root, proposer) and a list of transactions.
**Validator**: a node with stake that proposes and votes on blocks.
**State**: the map of all accounts, committed to by a Merkle root.

blocks.text: A user signs a transaction with their private key and sends it to any node. The node checks the signature, the nonce (to prevent replays) and the balance, adds it to its **mempool** (pending transactions), and **gossips** it to peers, so it spreads across the network in seconds.

In each slot, one **validator** is chosen (by stake-weighted rotation) as **proposer**. It picks transactions from its mempool (highest fees first), executes them to compute the new **state root**, and broadcasts the block.

Validators verify the block (signatures, execution, state root) and **vote**. A BFT-style protocol (like Tendermint or HotStuff) commits the block once validators holding **more than two thirds of the stake** have voted in two rounds (prepare, then commit). Once committed, the block is **final**: no conflicting block can gather the same supermajority without at least a third of validators provably misbehaving.
4) Storing state and serving light clients

Each node applies committed blocks to its **state database**, a Merkle tree (e.g. a Patricia trie) over accounts. The state root in each block header lets a **light client**, which only follows block headers, verify any balance with a short **Merkle proof** from a full node.

approach.text: Anyone can extend the chain; the longest chain wins.

challenges.text: Forks mean transactions are only probabilistically final — users wait for many confirmations, and finality can take an hour.

approach.text: Miners compete to solve a hash puzzle; the chain with the most cumulative work wins. Open participation without identities.

challenges.text: Enormous energy use, low throughput (~7-15 TPS), and still only probabilistic finality.

blocks.title: Proof of stake with BFT finality

approach.text: Validators lock up **stake**; proposers rotate, and blocks are finalised by a **two-thirds stake supermajority** of votes. Equivocation (voting for two conflicting blocks) is provable from signed votes and punished by **slashing** stake. This gives deterministic finality in seconds with tolerable energy use.

challenges.text: BFT voting is O(n²) messages, so the active validator set is limited (hundreds) or votes are aggregated with signature schemes like BLS.

blocks.text: Bigger and faster blocks increase throughput but also the bandwidth and hardware needed to run a node, which hurts decentralisation. Common techniques: **pipelining** consensus rounds, **parallel execution** of non-conflicting transactions, and moving most activity to **layer-2 rollups** that batch thousands of transactions and post compressed data plus proofs to the main chain.
Name the trilemma: security, decentralisation and scalability pull against each other. Every design choice trades one for another.

A new node downloads block headers, verifies the chain of hashes and validator signatures, then **state-syncs**: fetches a recent state snapshot in chunks from peers, verifying each against the state root, and replays only recent blocks. Peer discovery uses a DHT plus seed nodes; nodes limit connections per IP range to resist **eclipse attacks**.

quiz.question: Why do transactions carry a nonce?
options: To prevent the same signed transaction being replayed
quiz.explanation: Each account's nonce must increase, so an old transaction can't be resubmitted.

quiz.question: How many validators (by stake) must vote to finalise a block in BFT proof of stake?
quiz.explanation: A two-thirds supermajority tolerates up to one third faulty validators.

quiz.question: How does a light client verify its balance?
options: A Merkle proof checked against the state root in a block header
Ask a validator for a password
quiz.explanation: Proofs are small and verifiable against headers.

quiz.question: What is slashing?
options: Destroying stake of validators who provably misbehave
quiz.explanation: It makes attacks costly and accountable.
